introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography (0750), Paper 3, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2019. Duration: three and a quarter hours.**

Answer FOUR questions in all. Answer question ONE and three others, choosing ONE question from SECTION B and TWO from SECTION C. Question ONE carries thirty-one marks and the rest carry twenty-three marks each.

Only the required number of questions will be marked.

In answering questions on this paper, you are encouraged to refer to your own field and practical work where relevant. Credit will be awarded for such references.

Candidates are advised NOT to attempt the questions on field investigations if such an exercise has not been carried out.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Calculators are allowed.

Materials required: Topographic map, Graph Paper and two outline maps of Cameroon.

questions.enonce_markdown: 7. (a) Identify the main soil types of the Coastal Lowlands of Cameroon and briefly describe their characteristics. (9 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Coastal Lowlands (the Douala sedimentary basin, the Mount Cameroon foothills and the coast from Limbe to Kribi) are hot and very wet (rainfall often over 2,500 mm, and much more near Mount Cameroon), and have varied parent materials, so several soil types occur.

1. **Volcanic soils** (on the lava and ash of Mount Cameroon, around Buea, Tiko, Limbe and Muyuka). *Characteristics:* dark brown or black, loose, porous and well drained, rich in minerals (potassium, phosphates, magnesium) and organic matter, deep and fertile. *Use:* the large plantations of banana, oil palm, rubber and tea, and food crops.
2. **Alluvial soils** (along the lower valleys, flood plains and deltas of the Wouri, Mungo, Sanaga and Ndian rivers). *Characteristics:* loamy or silty, deposited by floods, fairly fertile and renewed each year, flat, but often waterlogged in the rainy season. *Use:* rice, vegetables, banana, cocoyam and food crops.
3. **Mangrove and swamp (hydromorphic) soils** (the Wouri estuary, the Rio del Rey and the Cameroon estuary creeks). *Characteristics:* grey to black, muddy, salty, waterlogged, rich in organic matter and clay, with an unpleasant smell, and acid if drained. *Use:* limited to fishing, salt making, firewood and mangrove products; difficult to farm.
4. **Sandy coastal soils** (beach ridges and sandy plains, for example near Limbe, Idenau and Kribi). *Characteristics:* light-coloured, coarse, loose, very permeable, low in humus and nutrients, easily leached and drought-prone. *Use:* coconut, cashew, cassava and tourism; poor for most crops.
5. **Ferralitic soils** (older sedimentary plains inland from the Douala basin). *Characteristics:* red or yellow, deep, strongly leached, acid, clayey and low in nutrients; the fertility is held in a thin humus layer under forest. *Use:* oil palm, rubber, cassava and plantain, with fertilizer and fallow.

(An annotated sketch map of the lowlands with these soils, named, earns marks.)

questions.enonce_markdown: (b) Examine the reasons for the socio-economic disparity between the Adamawa Plateau and the Coastal Lowlands of Cameroon. (9 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The **Coastal Lowlands** (Douala, Limbe, Kribi, Edea) are the most developed part of the country; the **Adamawa Plateau** (Ngaoundere and its region) is remote and less developed. The reasons are physical, historical, economic and political.

1. **Historical and colonial factors.** The coast was the first contact with Europeans (traders, missions, German then British and French rule). The colonial authorities built the port, the railways, the plantations and the first administrative and industrial centres there, and western schools and hospitals spread first on the coast.
2. **Physical advantages of the coast.** The sheltered estuary of the Wouri gave a natural harbour; the fertile volcanic and alluvial soils and the warm wet climate favour plantations of banana, oil palm and rubber. The Adamawa has a cooler, high plateau, with poorer ferruginous and leached soils that suit mainly extensive cattle rearing.
3. **Accessibility and transport.** The coast has the main seaports (Douala, Kribi, Limbe), the main airport and roads and railways joining it to the rest of the country, which attract investors. The Adamawa is far inland, several hundred kilometres from the sea; the railway reached Ngaoundere only in the 1970s and roads were long poor.
4. **Economic base.** The coast has industry (agro-industries, brewing, textiles, the oil refinery at Limbe and port industries), banking, commerce and oil activities, giving jobs and income. The Adamawa depends on **pastoralism and subsistence farming** with low incomes and little processing.
5. **Population and market size.** The large, urban population of the coast forms a big market and labour pool, while the Adamawa has few people and small markets.
6. **Services and investment.** Schools, hospitals, electricity and water are more available on the coast; government and private investment have concentrated in Douala and the neighbouring towns, so inequality has increased.
7. **Cultural and social factors.** Differences in the spread of western education, and in the traditional organisation of the economy, also played a part.

The result is a gap in income, employment, health, education and infrastructure between the two regions.

questions.enonce_markdown: (c) Examine the different strategies put in place by the government to bridge the gap between backward and prosperous regions in Cameroon. (6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The government has adopted several strategies for **regional balance**:

1. **Decentralisation.** The constitution of 1996 provides for regions and councils; laws on decentralisation (2004 and the General Code of Regional and Local Authorities of 2019) transfer powers and part of the national budget to regional and local councils so that each area plans its own development.
2. **Development strategies and plans.** National frameworks such as the Growth and Employment Strategy Paper (2010 to 2019) and the National Development Strategy 2020-2030 give priority to infrastructure, agriculture and industry in all regions, and local plans such as the **National Participatory Development Programme (PNDP)** finance village projects.
3. **Infrastructure in lagging regions.** Roads (for example the northern axis from Ngaoundere to Garoua and Maroua), bridges, dams (Lagdo, Lom Pangar), rural electrification and water supply projects open up backward areas and link them to the ports.
4. **Social services.** Building schools and health centres in remote areas, creating **priority education zones** in the north and east, and recruiting teachers and health workers for them.
5. **Support to agriculture and local industries.** Development agencies and schemes for cotton, rice (for example SEMRY in the Far North and UNVDA in the North West), livestock and agro-industries, the creation of industrial zones and incentives to investors outside Douala and Yaounde.
6. **Regional balance in public service.** A quota system for recruitment and scholarships so that disadvantaged regions are represented, and the creation of universities and administrative centres in all regions.

(Candidates should add an evaluation: results remain partial because of limited funds, corruption, slow transfer of resources and insecurity in some regions.)
